cards.example: Siempre me dice hola al entrar.
cards.note: The h is always silent in Spanish: OH-la.
In Spain the c before i sounds like the th in think: GRA-thyas. In Latin America it's an s.
Tap the r once with the tip of your tongue. The stress falls on the last syllable: fa-VOR.

cards.example: Siempre dice de nada con una sonrisa.
cards.note: Literally "of nothing". A d between vowels is soft, close to the th in "this".
The accent marks the stress: per-DÓN. Save lo siento for when you're truly sorry.

cards.example: Me gusta el agua con gas.
cards.note: Agua is feminine but takes el because it starts with a stressed a: el agua fría.

cards.example: Mi abuela vive en la casa azul.
cards.note: The s is always crisp like in "sun", never buzzing like a z. En casa means at home.

cards.example: Pedro es el amigo de mi hermano.
cards.note: A female friend is la amiga. A boyfriend or girlfriend is el novio or la novia.

cards.example: Vamos a comer a las dos.
cards.note: In Spain comer often means having lunch, and that tends to happen around 2 pm. The stress is on the last syllable: co-MER.
Spanish b and v sound the same. Between vowels the b is very soft, the lips barely touch.
The h is silent: a-BLAR. ¿Hablas inglés? asks whether someone speaks English.
The h is silent, so it sounds just like "oy" in "boy".
ñ sounds like the ny in canyon: ma-NYA-na. Por la mañana, on the other hand, means in the morning.
The stress is on the last syllable: a-YER. The day before yesterday is anteayer.
Before a masculine noun it shortens to buen: un buen día. For the adverb, as in I'm fine, use bien.
False friend: largo means long, not large. Before a singular noun grande shortens to gran: un gran día.
The ñ sounds like ny: pe-KE-nyo. In Latin America you'll often hear chico instead.
Lindo is very common in Latin America. The feminine form is bonita: una casa bonita.
A single r is tapped once. With rr, as in carro (car), you roll it longer.
Spanish vowels are short and clear: ba-RA-to. Nothing gets swallowed.
Question words carry an accent, even in indirect questions. Questions open with an upside-down mark: ¿...?
cu sounds like kw: KWAN-to. With feminine nouns it's cuánta, in the plural cuántos.

cards.example: Voy a la estación en taxi.
cards.note: Words ending in -ción are feminine and stressed on the last syllable: es-ta-THYON in Spain, es-ta-SYON in Latin America.
Say it KWEN-ta. In a restaurant, catch the waiter's eye and say: La cuenta, por favor.

cards.example: Tomo el desayuno a las ocho.
cards.note: Literally breaking the fast, just like English breakfast. Stress: de-sa-YU-no.
The h is silent: a-bi-ta-THYON. In a hotel you ask for una habitación doble or individual.
The j is a throaty sound like the ch in Scottish loch: tra-ba-HAR.
In the present tense the stem changes: entiendo, entiendes. No entiendo is one of the most useful phrases for beginners.

cards.example: Lo siento, no sé dónde está.
cards.note: Sé with an accent means I know, se without one is a pronoun. They sound exactly the same.
Adiós sounds rather final. Day to day people say hasta luego (see you later), even if they won't meet again.
